title: Starship Reaches Orbit for the First Time — Then Explodes After Splashdown
summary:
SpaceX's giant Starship rocket just did something it's never done before: it reached orbit. But the mission didn't go exactly as planned.

Soon after launch on September 28, one of Starship's 33 engines failed. The mission team spent a tense few minutes deciding whether to keep going. Then came the call: 'Go for orbit.' A short burst from the boosters pushed Starship into orbit, where it circled Earth at a highest point of 170 miles (275 kilometers) above the surface.

Starship successfully deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites — part of SpaceX's plan to improve internet service from space. But because of the engine problem, SpaceX decided not to leave the rocket in space for the full 10-hour mission. Instead, it splashed down in the Pacific Ocean after 3 hours and 8 minutes. Then it exploded with a fiery bang.

An explosive landing was always expected for Starship, and there were cheers during that part of the livestream. But SpaceX would probably have preferred to keep the rocket intact, like it did on Flight 13.

This was Starship's 14th flight and its first attempt to reach orbit. Before this, it had only flown suborbitally. Reaching orbit is a big step toward making Starship fully reusable.

The stakes are high: NASA wants to use a version of Starship to land astronauts on the Moon in early 2028. Today's engine issue leaves questions about whether SpaceX can meet that deadline.
why_it_matters: Giant rockets like Starship could someday carry people to the Moon and Mars, and the satellites it launches may bring faster internet to families in faraway places.

background_read: SpaceX (a private space company founded by Elon Musk) builds rockets and runs Starlink, a service that beams internet down from satellites in space.
NASA (the U.S. space agency) has a Moon program called Artemis, which aims to put astronauts back on the lunar surface — the last time people walked there was in 1972.
Starship is built to be reusable, meaning the rocket can fly again instead of being thrown away. Reusing rockets makes spaceflight much cheaper, which is why landing it safely matters so much.
Article_Structure: WHO: SpaceX, the company that builds Starship, and NASA, which wants to use Starship to reach the Moon.
WHAT: Starship reached orbit for the first time, released 26 Starlink satellites, then splashed down and exploded after about 3 hours.
WHERE: Launched from Earth, circled the planet at up to 170 miles high, and came down in the Pacific Ocean.
WHY: Reaching orbit is a major step toward a fully reusable rocket, but the failed engine leaves questions about whether NASA's Moon deadline can be met.

perspectives.description: SpaceX reached orbit for the first time and deployed its satellites, a big step toward a rocket that can fly again and again.
An engine failed on the way up, and the rocket was destroyed early, raising doubts about hitting NASA's Moon deadline.
Explosive endings after splashdown are expected during rocket testing, so engineers treat each flight as a lesson rather than a total success or failure.
